facts.title: Named After a Greek Region
facts.text: Magnesium takes its name from Magnesia, a district in Thessaly, Greece, where mineral-rich ores were found in antiquity. The same root also gave us the words manganese and magnet. The element was first isolated in 1808 by the English chemist Humphry Davy, who used electrolysis to separate it from magnesium oxide.

facts.title: It Burns With Blinding Light
facts.text: When ignited, magnesium burns with an intensely bright white flame that can reach roughly 3,100 degrees Celsius. This is why it was used in early photographic flash powder and in incendiary devices and flares. The light is so rich in ultraviolet that staring at it directly can damage your eyes.

facts.title: The Lightest Structural Metal
facts.text: With a density of about 1.74 grams per cubic centimeter, magnesium is the lightest metal used for everyday structural purposes, around 35 percent lighter than aluminum. Alloyed with elements like aluminum and zinc, it makes parts for cars, aircraft, laptops, and cameras where saving weight matters. The trade-off is that pure magnesium is relatively soft and flammable in finely divided form.

facts.title: Green Blood of Plants
facts.text: Every chlorophyll molecule has a single magnesium atom at its center, held within a ring structure that captures sunlight for photosynthesis. Without magnesium, plants cannot make the green pigment that converts carbon dioxide and water into sugars. In a real sense, almost all life on Earth depends on this metal sitting at the heart of leaves.

facts.title: Essential Inside Your Body
facts.text: An adult human body contains roughly 25 grams of magnesium, most of it stored in bones and muscles. It is required as a cofactor for more than 300 enzyme reactions, including those that make and use ATP, the cell's energy currency. It also helps regulate nerve signals, muscle contraction, and a steady heartbeat.

facts.title: The Eighth Most Common Element
facts.text: Magnesium is the eighth most abundant element in Earth's crust by mass and the fourth most common element in the planet as a whole. It is never found free in nature because it reacts readily, but it is locked into minerals such as dolomite, magnesite, and carnallite. The mineral olivine, rich in magnesium, makes up much of the Earth's mantle.

facts.title: A Sea Full of Magnesium
facts.text: Seawater is one of the largest practical sources of magnesium, containing about 1.3 grams of magnesium per liter. During World War II, factories extracted the metal directly from ocean water to build lightweight aircraft. Because the ocean is so vast, this supply is effectively inexhaustible.

facts.title: Medicine Cabinet Staple
facts.text: Magnesium compounds are common remedies: milk of magnesia is magnesium hydroxide used as an antacid and laxative, while Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate used in soaking baths. In hospitals, intravenous magnesium sulfate is a frontline treatment for eclampsia in pregnancy and for certain dangerous heart rhythms. These uses rely on magnesium's gentle, well-understood chemistry.

facts.title: Forged Inside Dying Stars
facts.text: Magnesium is created deep inside massive stars through nuclear fusion, particularly during carbon and neon burning late in a star's life. When such stars explode as supernovae, they scatter magnesium across space, where it later becomes part of new planets. The magnesium in your bones was literally cooked in a star billions of years ago.

facts.title: Fires You Cannot Put Out With Water
facts.text: A burning magnesium fire is notoriously dangerous because pouring water on it makes things worse. The hot metal splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, feeding the flames and risking an explosion. For this reason, magnesium fires must be smothered with dry sand or special Class D extinguishers rather than water or standard foam.
